column5: Question or concern
column7: Change wanted (optional: say what the module should say instead)

column5: assembly point (car park at the bottom of the Orangery) is taken from the trainer as a venue fact; please confirm it is current.

the trainer says to call 999 as well as raising the alarm. Many fire procedures have the alarm calling the Fire Service automatically or a manager making the call; confirm what your fire procedure says about who dials 999.
Confirm the assembly point is still the car park at the bottom of the Orangery, and that it is the same for the marquee and events.
Where the nearest break-glass call points and fire exits are in each department (your manager will show you).
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift.
the trainer says allergen orders should be prepared separately. Current Food Standards Agency guidance supports this; confirm it matches the venue's allergen procedure.
Where the accurate allergen information is kept for each menu (your manager will show you).
Who the chef or supervisor to tell is on each shift.
How allergen orders are flagged and prepared separately in the kitchen.
the trainer says "the person who makes the sale can be personally fined". This is right, but the law does not set a fixed small fine; please confirm you are happy with the wording used on the slides.
the trainer lists photo driving licence, passport and PASS hologram card as valid ID. Some premises also accept military ID or approved digital ID; confirm the venue's policy and update if needed.
the refusals log is good practice and usually part of the venue's age verification policy rather than a direct legal requirement; confirm.
The venue's written age verification policy and the refusals log: where it is kept and how to fill it in.
Which managers to call on each shift when someone pushes back after a refusal.
Whether the venue accepts any other ID beyond photo driving licence, passport and PASS-hologram cards.

the trainer says musculoskeletal injuries account for "roughly a third" of workplace ill-health "across the UK". HSE figures for work-related ill-health have put musculoskeletal disorders at around a quarter to a third in recent years; please confirm the current figure before relying on it. The slides say "about a third", as the trainer does.

the trainer says a full 50-litre keg "can weigh over 70kg". A full 50-litre keg is commonly nearer 60 to 65kg including the keg itself, depending on the keg. Please weigh a full one and confirm; the safe message (it is too heavy to throw around) does not change.
Where the sack barrows, keg trolleys and any lifting aids are kept (your manager will show you).
Which cellar ramps, drops, hatches and steps need extra care, and how they are lit.
Who to ask for a two-person lift on each shift.
none found, but please confirm the venue's own rules on who sharpens knives and how (the trainer only says a sharp knife is safer).
Where knives are stored, washed and dried in the kitchen (your manager will show you).
Which knives are used for which jobs, and where the non-slip board cloths are kept.
Where the first aid kit and the accident book are, in case of a cut.

the trainer says slips, trips and falls make up "around 30%" of workplace injuries in hospitality, are the most common cause of major injuries, lead to "hundreds of thousands" of lost working days and cost businesses "more than £500 million" a year. These are HSE-style headline figures but may be dated and are national rather than hospitality-specific; please confirm against current HSE statistics. The slides repeat them as the trainer states them.
Where wet floor signs, mops and spill kits are kept in each area (your manager will show you).
Which footwear each department expects.
Who your line manager is on each shift, and how to tell them.

the trainer says to write up the accident book "before the end of your shift". That is the venue's own rule rather than a legal deadline; please confirm it is what you want. RIDDOR reporting (to HSE) is the manager's job and is not taught in this trainer.
"behind most serious accidents there were usually lots of near-misses" echoes the well-known safety pyramid, which is a rule of thumb rather than a proven law; the slide softens it to "often".
Where the accident book is kept and how to complete it (your manager will show you).
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift.
Where the first aid kit and first aiders are.
none found. The trainer says to take a faulty appliance "out of use if you can"; confirm the venue's own method for doing this.
How to report a hazard you cannot fix, and who to tell on each shift (your manager will show you).
How to take faulty equipment out of use here (tag, sign, or unplug and tell a manager).
Known hazard areas in each department.
the trainer's emergency steps are brief (rinse, get first aid, report). For splashes the product's safety data sheet gives the exact first aid; confirm the venue's procedure matches.
Where the COSHH assessments and safety data sheets are kept (your manager will show you).
Which products the venue has approved for each job, and the correct dilutions.
Where the PPE is kept, and where the eyewash and first aid kit are.

colour-coding schemes vary. The trainer gives red for raw meat and green for salad and fruit "and so on". Many kitchens also use blue for raw fish, yellow for cooked meat, brown for vegetables and white for dairy and bakery; confirm the venue's scheme.
The venue's colour-coding scheme for boards, knives and equipment and where each is kept (your manager will show you).
Fridge layout and where raw meat and poultry are stored.
Where the handwash basins and sanitiser are.
the 20 second wash time is common guidance rather than a figure in the regulation; confirm it matches the venue food safety management system.
the 48 hours symptom-free rule matches Food Standards Agency guidance for vomiting and diarrhoea; confirm the venue policy says the same, and what applies to other illnesses.
Where the hand wash basins, soap and paper towels are in each food area
Where blue plasters are kept and who issues them
The venue rule on jewellery, perfume and uniform for food areas
Who you tell if you are ill, and how (phone, text or in person)
the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended parts of UK GDPR (including how requests for information are handled); the trainer does not mention it. Confirm nothing here is out of date.

the trainer says to report a breach to the General Manager. Confirm the venue procedure also covers telling the Information Commissioner's Office where required; no time limit is stated in the session.
the trainer says a breach can lead to a large fine. Kept as a general statement with no figure.
Who covers if the General Manager is away when a breach happens
Where booking sheets and function orders are locked away
Venue rules on screen locking, passwords and personal phones
How a guest asks to see their information, and how it reaches the General Manager

the trainer says to refuse alcohol to someone under the influence of drugs. Alcohol must not be sold to a drunk person (Licensing Act 2003, s.141); confirm the venue policy for someone you suspect is on drugs but not drunk.
the signs listed (frequent toilet trips, nosebleeds, jitteriness) can have innocent causes, including medical ones. The slides say they are signs to pass to a manager, not proof.
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them quietly
Where drug-related incidents are recorded
How often toilets are checked, and who does it
When the venue involves the police (the manager decides)
Whether the venue uses mattresses with handles, and who to ask for help from
How to report a strain or injury
Which rooms are turned on a regular schedule
Where trolleys are kept and what each is rated to carry
The maximum safe stack height for chairs
Where fire exits and keep-clear walkways are in each function room

the trainer says to have a colleague "foot" the ladder for higher or awkward tasks. HSE guidance prefers to secure (tie) a ladder, and footing is a fallback where tying is not possible; confirm the venue wording.

the trainer says ladders suit "short, light jobs". HSE guidance describes ladders as low-risk, short-duration equipment, with a duration given in guidance; no figure is quoted here, so confirm what the venue wants stated.
"surprising number of serious workplace falls" is the trainer's claim and no statistic is repeated.
Where ladders, step-ladders and any platforms or towers are kept
Who is trained or authorised to use them for each task
How to take a faulty ladder out of service and who to report it to
the trainer teaches user visual checks only. The session does not mention formal inspection or portable appliance testing, which is the venue's decision on risk; confirm the venue policy.
Where "out of use" labels are kept
Who is the competent person to report faulty equipment to
How the venue records formal testing of portable appliances, if it does
Which sanitiser and cloths each area uses
Where waste, recycling and linen go during service
Who covers the end-of-service clean in each area
the trainer gives the danger zone as roughly 8°C to 63°C. FSA guidance describes it as roughly 5°C to 63°C. The 8°C figure is the legal maximum for chilled food. Kept as the trainer says.
the trainer gives 75°C as a "common target" core temperature. FSA guidance describes 70°C for 2 minutes (or equivalent) as the standard; 75°C is a common venue target. Confirm the venue figure.
cooling "ideally within about 90 minutes" is industry guidance rather than a legal figure; confirm it matches the venue procedure.
hot food held at 63°C or above has limited legal exceptions (for example, short service periods); none are taught here.
Which probe thermometers are used and how they are calibrated and cleaned
Where temperature records are kept and who checks them
The venue's cooling method and where cooked food is chilled
Who you report a warm fridge or undercooked food to
the trainer says fridges run at 5°C or below. The legal maximum for chilled food is 8°C, and 5°C is the usual venue target (as in the temperature control session); confirm the venue figure.
freezers at -18°C or below is standard good practice for frozen food rather than a general legal figure; confirm the venue figure.
Where fridge and freezer temperature records are kept and who signs them
Which units serve which areas, and where the thermometers are
Who you report a warm unit to, and what happens to the food
Delivery put-away routine for chilled and frozen items

the trainer says research "consistently shows" a well-handled complaint can leave a guest more loyal. This is a widely quoted service-recovery finding, but the trainer gives no source, and the slides state it without citing a study.
allergic reactions, illness and injury must go to the Duty Manager; confirm the venue also expects these to be recorded (accident book, allergen incident log) after the guest has been looked after.
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them quickly
What staff are allowed to put right themselves (for example replacing a dish) before a manager is needed
Greeting and farewell wording the venue prefers, if it has a house style
Where menu and daily specials information is kept so staff can brush up before service

the trainer sends every concern to the Duty Manager, who decides what happens next. Confirm the venue has a named safeguarding lead and a clear route to the police (101) and children's services, so the Duty Manager is not left to decide alone.

the trainer lists warning signs only in outline (adult booking a room with an anxious or controlled young person, secrecy, little control over money, phone or movements). Confirm they match current guidance, such as that from the police and the NSPCC, before relying on the list.
the trainer says to keep concerns confidential. Confirm the venue also tells staff that confidentiality never stops a safeguarding report being passed to the Duty Manager or the police.
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them, including late at night
Whether the venue has a named safeguarding lead and a written reporting route beyond the Duty Manager
Where concerns are recorded and who is allowed to see the record

bullying has no single legal definition in England; the trainer's wording ("offensive, intimidating, malicious or humiliating") follows the ACAS description. Harassment under the Equality Act must relate to a protected characteristic, so the trainer's general wording is wider than the legal test.

the trainer says bullying and harassment have no place "even from a guest". Employer liability for harassment by guests and other third parties has been changing under the Employment Rights Act 2025; confirm what applies in October 2026 and that the venue's policy matches.

the trainer says concerns are handled confidentially and without anyone being treated badly. Confirm the venue's grievance procedure and any anti-victimisation wording are written down and match the ACAS Code of Practice on disciplinary and grievance procedures.
Who staff can go to first to raise a concern, and how to reach them
Where the grievance procedure is kept and who looks after it
Whether there is a confidential route when the concern is about the person's own manager

the trainer says employers must take "reasonable steps" to prevent sexual harassment, including by guests. From October 2026 the Employment Rights Act 2025 is expected to raise this to "all reasonable steps" and to strengthen protection for harassment by third parties. Confirm the wording and the date before the session is relied on.

the trainer says no one will be victimised for raising a genuine concern (Equality Act 2010, section 27). Confirm the venue has a written policy, a named person to report to and a record of the steps it takes.
Who to report to on each shift, including late at night at events and weddings
Where the venue's sexual harassment policy and risk assessment are kept
What a manager does when a guest is the problem (for example speaking to the guest, moving them, or asking them to leave)

the trainer's definition of indirect discrimination ("a rule or practice that unfairly disadvantages a particular group") is simplified. In law it is a provision, criterion or practice that puts people sharing a protected characteristic at a particular disadvantage, and that the employer or provider cannot justify. Confirm the simplified wording is acceptable for staff.
Who handles reasonable adjustment requests from guests, and what the venue can offer (for example large-print or read-aloud menus, step-free tables)
Where staff report discrimination, and who to go to if the concern involves a manager
The venue's equality and diversity policy and where staff can read it

the trainer says measuring spirits correctly is a legal requirement. It is for spirits sold by the measure (the measure sizes sold must be displayed and prescribed quantities used for some spirits), but not every drink or every cocktail is covered. Confirm the venue's measures and notices, and that wine is offered in the required sizes.
the trainer treats a chipped glass as a safety issue to be binned. Confirm the venue's broken and chipped glass procedure matches.
The venue's standard glass and garnish for each drink (the drinks spec)
Which spirit and wine measures the venue uses, and where the measures are displayed
How cask ales are kept and how long they settle before serving
Who to tell about a cloudy beer or a possible line or cellar fault

the trainer does not say the venue's alarm must be tested and maintained, or that cylinder changes need trained, authorised staff. Confirm the venue's CO2 detector is installed, tested and serviced on a schedule, and who is authorised to change cylinders.

the trainer treats "if the alarm sounds, do not go in" as the rule. Confirm the venue has a written emergency procedure for a collapsed person in the cellar (call 999, do not enter to rescue) and that staff have been told it.
Where the cellar gas alarm is, what it sounds like and who to tell when it goes off
The correct procedure for changing gas cylinders here, and who is trained to do it
Where the cellar vents are and the rule for keeping the cellar door open or closed
Who to report a gas leak or damaged cylinder to, and the out-of-hours contact

the trainer says falls from height are the single biggest cause of workplace deaths in the UK, and cause thousands of serious injuries. HSE statistics have long listed falls from height as the biggest cause of fatal workplace injuries; confirm the latest HSE annual figures before this wording is relied on.
the trainer is for maintenance and housekeeping staff. Confirm the venue has rules on who may use towers and platforms, and on who inspects ladders and steps.
What access equipment the venue has (step-ladders, platform steps, towers) and where it is kept
Who is allowed to use the higher equipment, and who inspects it
Who to report unsafe access or damaged equipment to
the trainer says some bulbs, such as fluorescent tubes, need special disposal. Confirm which types the venue uses and the correct waste route (for example separate collection for fluorescent tubes).

the trainer says to isolate the light "where you can". Confirm who is competent to isolate a circuit at the venue, and that staff are not expected to touch wiring or open fittings beyond swapping a bulb.
Who is allowed to change bulbs, and which fittings (high ceilings, specialist fittings) are for maintenance only
Where step-ladders are kept, and where spare bulbs of the correct type are stored
Who in maintenance to report a damaged, scorched or loose fitting to
How old bulbs and fluorescent tubes are disposed of here

the trainer says cool a burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. This matches current NHS and St John Ambulance first aid advice, but please confirm it matches your first aid provider's training.
Where the first aid kit is kept in the kitchen
Who the first aiders are on each shift
Where hot oil and fryer procedures are written down

the trainer says slips are "the most common accident in our industry". HSE reports slips and trips as the most common cause of major injury across all workplaces, but the hospitality claim is not verified here. The slides say "one of the biggest causes" only.
Where wet floor signs, mops, absorbent and spill kits are kept
The correct clean-up method and kit for oil, grease and broken glass
Who to report recurring wet spots to on each shift

Martyn's Law (the Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025) places new duties on venues, depending on capacity, with a phased start. Please confirm whether and when it applies to the venue and whether this trainer needs updating.

police advice on suspicious items is often summarised as HOT (Hidden, Obviously suspicious, Typical). The trainer's "do not touch" and alert-the-Duty-Manager approach is taught as written; confirm it matches current counter-terrorism guidance.
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them quickly
Where a pen and paper or a threat call checklist is kept near the main phones
How the Duty Manager will signal an evacuation
Run, Hide, Tell is the national police and counter-terrorism advice and is taught as the trainer states it. Please confirm it is still the current wording.
Martyn's Law (Terrorism (Protection of Premises) Act 2025) may place duties on the venue depending on capacity. Confirm whether and when it applies.
Likely escape routes and safe places to hide from each area of the venue, including the marquee
Which doors can be locked or barricaded from the inside
How staff are told of a lockdown

for choking the trainer says encourage coughing, then back blows and abdominal thrusts if trained. Current first aid guidance is back blows first, then abdominal thrusts; confirm with your first aid provider.

burn cooling, firm direct pressure for heavy bleeding, and 999 plus CPR for someone unresponsive and not breathing normally match current NHS and Resuscitation Council advice, but please confirm with your first aid trainer.
Where each first aid kit is kept
Who the first aiders are on each shift
Where and how incidents and first aid are recorded

the trainer says serving food past its use-by date is "breaking the law". This is broadly correct (food past its use-by is treated as unsafe and must not be sold), but confirm you are happy with the wording.
The venue's labelling system and what must go on a label
Where and how discarded food is recorded
Who the supervisor is on each shift
No  items found. Confirm the pest control arrangements named in siteNotes.
The pest control contractor and how to contact them
Who to report pest signs to on each shift
Where bin areas and external doors are, and how they are checked
No  items found.
Where the broken-glass bins and containers are kept
Where each waste stream goes: general, mixed recycling, glass and used cooking oil
Where the brush and dustpan, and the ice scoop, are kept behind the bar

the trainer says PPE is the last line of defence after reducing the hazard. This matches the hierarchy of controls and the Personal Protective Equipment at Work Regulations 1992 (employer provides PPE free where risks remain). Please confirm the venue provides PPE free of charge.

the trainer lists non-slip footwear as PPE. Slip-resistant footwear is often provided as PPE in hospitality, but whether it counts as PPE depends on whether the employer requires it for the work; please confirm the venue's position.
What PPE is issued for each department and where it is kept
Who to report damaged, worn out or missing PPE to
Which tasks need cut-resistant gloves, chemical gloves or eye protection
taking callers' names and numbers involves personal data. Confirm the venue's data protection practice (see the data-protection session) covers how enquiry details are logged and kept.
The venue's standard phone greeting
Where wedding and event enquiries are logged
Who handles call-backs for each type of enquiry and how quickly
How bookings are checked (system or book) and where accessible tables and highchairs are
Which specials are mentioned at the table each service
Who the duty manager is on each shift and how to call them quickly
What a front-line team member is allowed to offer to put things right

serve from the left, clear and pour from the right is traditional service etiquette, stated in the trainer as a general rule rather than a legal requirement; confirm it matches the venue's house style.
Whether the venue's house style differs from the general serving and clearing rule
Tray and plate-carrying standards used at the venue
Current specials, signature dishes and wine pairings the team should know
Where the running order and special requests are kept for each event
Who leads the event team on the day
the trainer's "record any refusal in the log" is venue practice rather than a legal requirement; confirm the venue keeps a refusals log and where.
the trainer says "protects our licence"; confirm the venue is content with this wording alongside its premises licence conditions.
Where the refusals log is kept and how an entry is written
How taxis are arranged for guests at the venue
Who the duty manager is on each shift
No  items. The trainer correctly says lone working is not banned.
Who to tell, and how to check in, when opening or closing alone
How help is raised quickly at each site (phone, alarm, nearest colleague)
Which tasks are not to be done alone

the trainer lists ventilate, turn off at the valve, evacuate and call. Gas network advice is to call from outside the building and not to operate any electrical switch, including doorbells, so please confirm the venue's agreed order of actions and that the evacuation point is known.
carbon monoxide warning signs (yellow or orange flames, soot) are stated as in the trainer; confirm the venue has carbon monoxide alarms where needed.
Where the gas shut-off valves and the meter are in each kitchen and building
Whether there is an emergency gas shut-off or interlock for the kitchen, and where it is
Who to report appliance faults to
No  items; the trainer's heavy-low, light-high advice matches standard manual handling guidance.
Where steps and kick stools are kept in each store
Shelf load ratings where known
Which exits and routes must never be blocked in each store

the trainer's answer sheet for question 4 marks "Raised high" as correct, which contradicts the trainer text (forearms roughly horizontal). This session uses "Roughly horizontal" as the right answer; please confirm the answer sheet is a typo.
Who arranges a workstation assessment and how to ask for one
Whether footrests and other equipment are available

the trainer gives hot water above 50°C and cold water below 20°C. HSE guidance gives hot water at 50°C or above at outlets (stored at 60°C or above) and cold below 20°C; confirm against the venue's own risk assessment.
the trainer gives roughly 20°C to 45°C as the growth range, which matches HSE; confirm the venue wording.
the trainer says people catch it by breathing in droplets, not by drinking the water. HSE notes that inhaling droplets is the usual route; confirm the wording is acceptable.
Who is responsible for the water risk assessment and temperature checks
How and when little-used rooms and outlets are flushed and recorded
Who in maintenance to report water warning signs to
Whether and how the hot tub water is tested and treated
the trainer says alcohol gel does not reliably kill norovirus, which matches NHS and FSA advice; confirm the venue sickness policy matches.
Who to call and how to report sickness before a shift
The venue's sickness clean-up kit, where it is kept and what disinfectant it contains
Who confirms staff are clear to return to food work after 48 hours symptom-free

the trainer says to encourage a puncture wound to bleed. Current NHS and UKHSA first aid for a needlestick is to wash with soap and running water, and not to suck or scrub the wound; confirm the venue is happy with "encourage it to bleed gently".

the trainer says to use a "tool or a sharps container, or a brush and pan". Confirm the venue procedure for picking up found needles, as many sites ask staff not to handle them at all and to call a trained person.
Where the bodily-fluid spill kits, gloves and sharps bins are kept
Who to report a sharps find or injury to, and how it is recorded
Where staff get prompt medical advice after a needlestick or splash

the trainer says to lay a person in shock down and keep them warm. Current first aid guidance is to lay them down with legs raised if possible; the trainer does not mention raising legs, so it is left out. Confirm this suits the venue.
the trainer says "grounds machinery" as one cause. Confirm the venue is happy to name it, as it is for the Maintenance team.
Where the first aid kits and any bleed-control kit are kept
Who the trained first aiders are on each shift
Which staff are trained to use a trauma dressing or tourniquet, if any
How to book the venue's first aid training
the trainer says chainsaws need "proper certificated training". Confirm the venue's requirement (for example NPTC or Lantra chainsaw certificates) and who holds them.

the trainer lists typical PPE (eye protection, ear defenders, gloves, boots, close-fitting clothing, chainsaw trousers). Confirm the exact kit required for each machine in the venue's risk assessment.
Which grounds machines each person is trained and authorised to use
Where PPE, including eye protection and ear defenders, is kept
Who to report faulty machines to, and how they are taken out of use
Where fuel is stored and where refuelling is done
the trainer mentions a "banksman". Confirm whether the venue has a banksman arrangement or relies on reversing aids.
Where vehicles unload, the marked walkways and any banksman arrangements
Where the car park and delivery area are poorly lit or uneven
Where high-visibility clothing is kept
Which routes and ramps to treat with extra care with cages and trolleys
confirm 116 123 is still the Samaritans free number and that it is open day and night.
Who staff can speak to at the venue about wellbeing, and how to arrange a private chat
Whether the venue has an employee assistance line or wellbeing support
Break arrangements and where staff can take them
Where a colleague can rest or express milk in private, and how to ask for it
Which manager carries out the specific risk assessment in each department
Where the probe thermometers are kept and where buffet temperature records are written
Which sneeze screens, serving utensils and labels the venue uses for wedding and event buffets
75°C core temperature is given in the trainer only as an example of a critical limit. Confirm it matches the venue's own HACCP plan (FSA guidance also allows other time and temperature combinations).
the trainer says many venues run this through the "Safer Food, Better Business" pack; confirm the venue still uses the current version.
The venue's own HACCP plan or Safer Food, Better Business pack and where it is kept
Where temperature logs and cleaning diaries are filled in, and who to report a warm fridge or delivery to
the trainer says musculoskeletal injuries make up "around a third of workplace ill-health". Confirm against the latest HSE statistics, or soften to "a large share".
Where trolleys, sack barrows and other lifting aids are kept
Who to report a strain or twinge to on each shift
the trainer uses "vulnerable adults". Current terminology in England is often "adults at risk". Confirm whether the venue wants the wording changed; it is kept as the trainer has it.
Who the Duty Manager is on each shift and how to reach them
Where a note of a concern is written and kept confidentially
Modern Slavery Helpline number 08000 121 700 is quoted from the trainer. Confirm it is still current and that the service is still the right one to point staff to.
Who the Duty Manager and General Manager are on each shift and how to reach them
the trainer gives adult choking steps only. Technique for babies and young children is different and is not covered; confirm the venue wants that stated or taught elsewhere.

the trainer says to call 999 if the blockage does not clear quickly. Current Resuscitation Council UK / St John Ambulance guidance for a severe choke is to call 999 once back blows and abdominal thrusts have not worked, or earlier if someone else can call. Confirm the trainer's wording matches the first aid provider's current guidance.
Who the first aiders are on each shift
Where the first aid kit and defibrillator are, and who calls 999
confirm the trainer's figures against the current Resuscitation Council UK guidelines at the next review.
Where the nearest defibrillator (AED) is in each part of the venue
Who calls 999 and who fetches the AED when a colleague is doing CPR
Who to report a suspicious message to on each shift, and how
Who is allowed to approve changes to supplier bank details, and the known phone number used to check them

the trainer says the law protects people who raise concerns "in good faith". Since 2013 the legal test is a reasonable belief that the disclosure is in the public interest, not good faith (good faith can only affect compensation). Wording kept as the trainer has it; confirm whether to change.
the trainer says concerns go to the manager or General Manager, then the business owners. Confirm the venue's whistleblowing policy names the same route.
Who the business owners are and how to contact them if a concern involves a manager or the General Manager
Where the grievance procedure is kept
Your manager will show you the end-of-service switch-off routine for your area.
Who to tell about leaks, broken seals or heating and lighting left on in empty areas.

the trainer says to give a second dose after 5 minutes if there is no improvement and another injector is available. This matches current Resuscitation Council UK and NHS guidance as far as known, but please confirm with your first aid trainer.
the trainer says to lie the person down with legs raised, or sit up if struggling to breathe. Current first aid guidance varies on raising the legs; confirm the wording with your first aid provider.
Where the first aid kit is, and who the first aiders are.
What to say on the 999 call about where to send the ambulance, and who meets it at the entrance.

the trainer refers to "PCI" standards. PCI DSS is the card industry's data security standard, set by the card schemes rather than by law; the slides only say card payments come with rules. Please confirm the venue's card provider requirements.
The venue's cash-handling procedure.
Who authorises refunds, voids and manual key-entry on each shift.
Who to report suspected fraud or counterfeit notes to.

the trainer says keep people away from an unattended bag and report it to a manager. Confirm the venue's own suspicious-item procedure (for example when to call 999 or evacuate) and add it to the site notes.
How a guest's identity is verified at your desk.
Who the duty manager is to alert about suspicious behaviour or unattended items.
Where the key and keycard controls are kept.
the trainer says to follow "the sharps procedure". Confirm the venue has a written procedure (including what to do after a needlestick or cut) and add it to the site notes.
The venue's sharps procedure: who to tell and how a sharp is made safe.
Where gloves are kept and which laundry chemicals are used, with their COSHH information.
Where trolleys are kept and any slopes or lifts to take care in.

the trainer says to report weapons, drugs or signs a guest may be vulnerable to your manager, who will decide what to do. Confirm the venue's procedure, including when to call 999 or the police straight away, and the safeguarding route for a vulnerable guest.
How master keys are signed out and kept secure.
How a guest is verified when someone asks to be let in.
Which manager to report concerning finds to, including out of hours.
Who confirms you are trained and competent on each tool.
How faulty tools are tagged and reported, and where tools are stored.
